scenario: AITA for telling my sister that her beating breast cancer was not impressive and not inspirational? | Three years ago my older sister was diagnosed with breast cancer. Within six months her cancer was cleared. She had minor radiAtion and then hormone therapy afterwards. She is 100% fine and healthy no need for surgery. We all came together and supported her during this time. Now, the thing has been is that she hasn’t stopped to remind us constantly about how she is a cancer survivor. And has made it her identity. She has since plastered it all over social media. I don’t mind it because I can choose to ignore it. But this holiday season she was insufferable. My breaking point happened when my dad who has been dealing with nerve problems was telling us how physical therapy wasn’t working for him and he will likely need to get surgery. My sister started bringing up her cancer story again. I snapped and told her that her surviving breast cancer was not impressive nor inspiration, it has a survival rate of 96% and to stop making everything about her story. My sister walked out of the room. I thought my family would back me up but instead my parents backed up my sister. My dad didn’t say anything but he was on my sisters side. I don’t know maybe what I said wasn’t the nicest way but I don’t think I was wrong in what I said.

prediction.raw: 1. I think you were wrong in how you approached the situation. While it's understandable that you might feel frustrated with your sister's constant reminders about her cancer experience, telling her that her survival was "not impressive" and "not inspirational" was hurtful and dismissive of her feelings. Breast cancer is a life-altering and traumatic experience, regardless of the survival rate. Your sister's experience and emotions are valid, and it's not up to you to decide what is or isn't impressive or inspirational. It's also important to consider the context of the conversation. Your dad was sharing his struggles with nerve problems, and your sister's response, although perhaps insensitive, was likely a way of trying to relate and offer support. Your reaction, on the other hand, came across as insensitive and dismissive of your sister's experience. A more empathetic approach would have been to acknowledge your sister's experience and feelings while also gently pointing out that the conversation was about your dad's struggles. You could have said something like, "I understand that you're trying to relate, but let's focus on Dad's situation right now. We're all worried about him and want to support him." Remember, empathy and understanding are key in situations like this. It's not about being "right" or "wrong," but about being kind, compassionate, and supportive of those around you.
